unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9 — the final unit of Year 4! This unit is all about places, people, and plans. You will learn the words we use to talk about travelling: the airport, the station, the museum, the capital city, and much more. You will meet the people we find in busy places, like the customer at a shop and the workers in an office. Most of all, you will learn how to make plans — how to invite a friend, how to say what you are going to do, and how to give clear directions. By the end, you will be able to plan a whole trip in English, just like Amal and Noah do in this unit's story when they explore the city of Mombasa.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary file. Learn a small group of place words each day.
Work through the Grammar file. Six lessons carry the eight patterns of this unit — take one at a time.
Read the Story file, “The Day We Got Lost in Mombasa”, and answer the questions.
Work through the four skills below in order: Reading & Listening → Speaking → Writing → Activities.
Finish with the Self-Assessment to check what you have learned this year.

readings.title: A Trip to the Capital
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Last month, my family took a trip to the capital city, and I could not wait to see the tall buildings I had only seen in photos. First, we went to the big station and waited for the train under a large clock. The platform was noisy with travellers carrying suitcases and baskets, and a vendor sold warm bread near the entrance. When the train arrived, we found seats near the window and watched the horizon rush past as green fields slowly turned into rooftops.
In the city there was so much to see! We visited a museum full of old maps and tools, and a kind guide showed us a stone that was thousands of years old. Then we walked through a busy neighbourhood, past shops, offices, and a tall building with a glass elevator that seemed to touch the sky. Tourism brings many people to the capital, so the streets were full, and we held hands so we would not get separated in the crowd.
At the end of the day, we ate at a small restaurant near the entrance of the market. We shared rice, grilled fish, and cold juice while we talked about everything we had seen. My little brother fell asleep before we even reached the station for our journey home. I was tired, but I would like to go again next year, and next time I want to visit the capital's tallest office tower too.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: Living Near the Equator
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Kenya sits close to the equator, the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth. Near the equator, the sun is very strong and the days are warm all year, so people often wear light clothes and drink plenty of water. Farmers still grow crops such as maize, tea, and coffee, even when the afternoon heat is at its highest. Children walk to school in the early morning, before the sun climbs too high above the horizon.
People still build, travel, and work hard here. In the towns, workers repair roads and offices, and in the countryside, families care for animals and fields. Trains run on the railroad, ships arrive at the coast, and factories make goods for the whole nation, from cloth and shoes to tools for the farm. Lorries carry these goods from the factories to markets in every neighbourhood, so shops in small towns and big cities both stay busy.
Whether you live in a small neighbourhood or a big capital, there is always a place to go and a plan to make. Some families plan a trip to the museum or the mall at the weekend, while others simply enjoy a walk to watch the sun set beyond the fields. Living near the equator means long, warm days and plenty of time to explore.

readings.title: Making a Plan (listening script)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Nora: “We're going to explore the capital on Saturday, aren't we?”
Leo: “Yes! I've been looking forward to it all week. First we are going to the museum — I want to see the old maps and the model train.”
Nora: “That sounds wonderful. Then what?”
Leo: “Then we would like to try the new restaurant near the station. My cousin says they serve the best grilled fish in the city.”
Nora: “Shall we go by train, or take the bus from our neighbourhood?”
Leo: “Let's take the train. It's faster, and we can watch the horizon from the window.”
Nora: “Good idea! I'd love to! Let's arrive early so we have more time to look around before lunch. I'm so excited!”
Leo: “Me too! I'll bring the map so we don't get lost near the station.”
Nora: “And I'll bring my notebook so I can write down three facts from the museum.”
Leo: “Perfect. Saturday cannot come fast enough!”
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: Directions at the Mall (listening script)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
“Welcome to the mall! We hope you enjoy your visit today. To find the bookshop, take the elevator to the second floor. While you wait for the lift, you can see the fountain in the hallway below.
When the doors open on the second floor, turn left and walk down the long hallway, past the toy shop and the phone stand. The bookshop is near the entrance, next to the juice stand, and you will see its blue sign from a distance.
If you would like a snack first, the restaurant is on the first floor, close to the main entrance. For families with small children, the play area is just past the elevator, on the right.
Please walk carefully — the floor can be slippery near the juice stand, especially after it rains. If you need help finding a shop, ask any worker wearing a red badge; they will be happy to give you directions.
The mall closes at nine o'clock this evening, so please finish your shopping in good time. Thank you for visiting, and we hope to see you again soon!”

readings.title: The Day We Got Lost in Mombasa
readings.setting: Mombasa, a lively coastal city near the equator
readings.passageScript:
“We're going to the capital, aren't we?” asked Amal, holding her small travel bag.
“Not today,” said her uncle with a smile. “We're visiting Mombasa! It's a special city by the ocean. There's a museum, a station, and even a big restaurant near the sea.”
Amal and her cousin Noah were excited. It was their first time travelling without their parents. Their uncle was in charge.
They arrived at the station earlier than planned. “Let's buy some juice while we wait,” said Noah.
At the juice stand, the customer in front of them bought three bottles. “Take your time,” said the seller kindly.
Noah whispered, “This place is so busy. The neighbourhood feels different from ours.”
Amal nodded. “It's bigger. More tourism, maybe. Look at all the visitors!”
When their train came, they found seats near the window. “I want to see the horizon,” said Amal. “I love how the sea meets the sky.”
In Mombasa, the air was hotter, and the streets were full of colour. “First stop,” said her uncle, “the museum.”
Inside, they saw old tools, maps, and animal bones. A guide pointed to the wall. “This was found near the equator,” he explained. “The heat there is strong, but people still build and work hard.”
Amal and Noah took photos. “Now, let's go to the mall before lunch,” said her uncle.
At the mall, they looked for gifts and rode the elevator for fun. “We went up to the fourth floor faster than I thought!” said Noah.
After that, they stopped at a restaurant. “Would you like to try local fish, or chicken and rice?” asked her uncle.
“I'd like the chicken,” said Noah. “Me too!” added Amal.
“You two always agree,” he said, laughing.
“I feel hungry already,” said Amal.
The waiter walked them to their table. “The entrance is beautiful,” said Amal, looking at the painted doors.
After lunch, her uncle had a quick call at the office where he once worked. “Wait by the shop near the hallway, okay?”
“Okay,” said Amal. “We'll stay carefully nearby.”
But the shop was full of wonderful souvenirs — little aeroplanes for the airport, capital city keychains, and even a tiny model railroad!
Noah's eyes grew wide. “Let's just look at that shop across the street.”
“But Uncle said to wait,” Amal warned.
“It won't take long,” said Noah.
They crossed the road and looked around. But when they turned back, the building looked different. The entrance had a blue sign now, not a green one.
“This isn't the place!” said Amal, her heart beating fast. “Where's the hallway? Where's the office?”
They were lost.
Amal took a slow breath. “Let's not panic. Let's ask someone at the rental stand,” she said.
A kind woman there smiled. “I saw your uncle go that way. Take the elevator up. His office is on the second floor.”
They thanked her and followed her directions. Carefully, they stepped into the elevator and pressed the button.
When the door opened, they saw their uncle at the end of the hallway.
“You're going to give me grey hair!” he said, but then he smiled. “You're safe — that's what matters most.”
“We were just curious,” said Noah, looking down.
“Curiosity is good,” Uncle replied gently. “But you must stay careful in busy places, and keep to the plan.”
Back at the train station, they waited with cold drinks.
“We saw so many places today,” said Amal. “The factories, the market, even the coast.”
“I liked the museum the best,” said Noah. “It teaches more than the mall does.”
Uncle nodded. “That's the difference between shopping and learning.”
“Would you like to travel again?” he asked.
“Yes!” they shouted together.
“Maybe next time we'll see the airport,” said Amal.
“Or climb a hill near the equator,” added Noah.
They laughed, feeling tired but happy. As the train pulled away, Amal looked out at the setting sun. “I can still see the ocean,” she said softly, “far away on the horizon.”

comprehension.question: Where did the family go first, before the train arrived?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They went to the big station and waited there for the train.
comprehension.explanation: The second sentence of the text says they went to the big station and waited for the train.

comprehension.question: Which three places did the family visit inside the capital city?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They visited a museum, a busy neighbourhood, and a small restaurant.
comprehension.explanation: The writer lists the museum of old maps, the busy neighbourhood of shops, and the restaurant near the market.

comprehension.question: Which sentence tells you why the streets of the capital were so full?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The sentence is: Tourism brings many people to the capital, so the streets were full.
comprehension.explanation: The word so joins the cause, tourism, to its result, the crowded streets.

comprehension.question: How does the text explain what the equator is?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The equator is the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth.
comprehension.explanation: The opening sentence defines the equator straight after naming it.

comprehension.question: What do the factories make, and who are the goods for?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The factories make goods for the whole nation.
comprehension.explanation: The third sentence pairs the trains and ships with the factories that supply the nation.

comprehension.question: In the listening script, which place are Nora and Leo going to visit first?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They are going to the museum first, and the restaurant afterwards.
comprehension.explanation: Leo says First we are going to the museum, then names the restaurant as the next stop.

comprehension.question: Which words show that Nora and Leo feel excited about Saturday?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Nora says I'm so excited, and Leo answers Me too.
comprehension.explanation: Both speakers use short feeling phrases, so the excitement is stated rather than guessed.

comprehension.question: How do the mall directions tell you to reach the second floor?
comprehension.correctAnswer: You take the elevator to the second floor.
comprehension.explanation: The first instruction after the welcome names the elevator and the floor.

comprehension.question: After the elevator, which way do you turn to reach the bookshop?
comprehension.correctAnswer: You turn left and walk down the long hallway.
comprehension.explanation: The directions give the turn and then the hallway before naming the shop near the entrance.

comprehension.question: Which city did the children visit, and what makes it special in the story?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They visited Mombasa, a special city by the ocean.
comprehension.explanation: The uncle corrects Amal at the start and describes Mombasa as a city beside the sea.

comprehension.question: Why did Amal and Noah end up lost near the office?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They crossed the road to another shop instead of waiting as they were told.
comprehension.explanation: Noah suggests looking at the shop across the street, and the entrance they return to has a different sign.

comprehension.question: Which place did Noah like best, and what reason did he give?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Noah liked the museum best because it teaches more than the mall.
comprehension.explanation: Near the end Noah names the museum and gives his reason in the same breath.

grammar.title: Would like to
grammar.explanation: “Would like to” is a polite way to say what you want, or to invite someone to do something. It is a kinder, softer way of saying “I want to”, and it keeps you friendly and respectful.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use: would like to + the base verb (the plain form of the action).
“I would like to visit the museum.”
“She would like to play football.”
To invite someone, turn it into a question: “Would you like to come with us?”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “I would like visit the park.” ✗
Fix: Do not drop the little word to — write “I would like to visit the park.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Think: would like to + do. The word “to” builds a tiny bridge across to the action.
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with “would like to” and the verb in brackets. | She ______ (visit) her grandparents this weekend. | They ______ (play) football after school. | ______ you ______ (join) us for lunch? Answer key: 1) would like to visit; 2) would like to play; 3) Would you like to join.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Going to (Future Plans)
grammar.explanation: We use “going to” for plans we have already decided on. It tells the listener what we intend to do later.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use: subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb.
I → am: “I am going to visit my aunt.”
He / She / It → is: “She is going to join the team.”
You / We / They → are: “We are going to explore the capital.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “I going to play.” ✗
Fix: Keep the to be word in place — write “I am going to play.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: “Going to” is a road sign pointing at the future. Ask yourself: have I already planned it?
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with the correct form of “going to”. | They ______ (visit) the museum next week. | I ______ (have) a party on Saturday. | She ______ (read) a new book this month. Answer key: 1) are going to visit; 2) am going to have; 3) is going to read.

grammar.title: Comparative and Superlative Adverbs
grammar.explanation: Adverbs tell us how an action is done, such as quickly or carefully. Comparing them shows that one action is done more, or the most, and that makes a description exact.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Short adverbs of one syllable add -er and -est: fast → faster → fastest.
Adverbs ending in -ly take more and most: carefully → more carefully → most carefully.
A few are irregular: well → better → best.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “He arrived more fast than me.” ✗
Fix: “Fast” is short, so add -er — write “He arrived faster than me.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Comparative compares two things (-er or more). Superlative crowns the best of all (-est or most).
grammar.practice: Write the correct form of the adverb in brackets. | She sings ______ (loud) than her sister. | Out of all the students, he works the ______ (hard). | This book reads ______ (easy) than the last one. Answer key: 1) louder; 2) hardest; 3) easier.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Present Continuous for Plans
grammar.explanation: The present continuous (am/is/are + verb-ing) usually means happening right now. It also describes plans that are already arranged, especially when we say when.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing, plus a future time word.
“We are visiting the factories next week.”
“She is studying for her test this weekend.”
“I am meeting my friends tomorrow.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “We are plan a visit.” ✗
Fix: Add -ing to the verb — write “We are planning a visit.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Call it the now-and-later tense. Picture the action, add a time word, and it becomes a plan.
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with the present continuous form. | I ______ (visit) my grandmother this weekend. | They ______ (watch) a new show tonight. | We ______ (plan) a picnic for Saturday. Answer key: 1) am visiting; 2) are watching; 3) are planning.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Imperatives (Instructions)
grammar.explanation: Imperatives are the verbs we use to tell someone what to do. They carry directions, instructions and friendly commands, which is exactly what you need when you show a visitor around a busy building.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Start with the base verb and leave out “you”: “Take the elevator.” not “You take the elevator.”
Add please to sound polite: “Please check the map.”
For a no, begin with don't: “Don't run in the hallway.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “Not touch that.” ✗
Fix: A negative command begins with don't — write “Don't touch that.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Imagine a friendly captain giving an order. She never says “You go”; she simply says “Go!”
grammar.practice: Fill in each blank with the correct imperative; the verb is in brackets. | ______ the book on the table. (put) | ______ your homework before dinner. (finish) | ______ the lights when you leave. (turn off) Answer key: 1) Put; 2) Finish; 3) Turn off.

grammar.title: Question Tags, Expressions of Emotion, and Sentence Starters
grammar.explanation: Three friendly conversation tools meet in this lesson. A question tag checks that someone agrees, a feeling phrase shares how you are, and a pronoun or sentence starter opens your idea neatly.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Question tags: a positive sentence takes a negative tag — “You're happy, aren't you?”
A negative sentence takes a positive tag — “They don't like it, do they?”
Match the tag to the subject pronoun — “She can swim, can't she?”
Feelings: use I'm + feeling — “I'm excited!” or “I'm nervous.”
You can also say I feel + feeling — “I feel hungry.” To agree, say “Me too!”
Pronouns and starters: swap a name for a pronoun — “Maya likes it.” becomes “She likes it.”
Open a plan with a starter — “Let's go to the museum.” or “We need a map.”
I is the doer and me is the receiver — “I like it.” and “She gave me a book.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Tags: “You're happy, are you?” ✗ A positive sentence needs a negative tag, so write “You're happy, aren't you?” ✓
Feelings: “I happy.” ✗ The feeling needs the verb, so write “I'm happy.” ✓
Pronouns: “Me want to go.” ✗ “Me” cannot be the doer, so write “I want to go.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Picture a seesaw for tags: sentence up, tag down. Feelings always ride on “I'm”. Pronouns are shortcuts, and starters are the keys that unlock your first line.
grammar.practice: Part A — choose the correct question tag. | You're coming to the party, ______? (aren't you / are you) | They don't like chocolate, ______? (do they / don't they) | She's your friend, ______? (is she / isn't she) | Part B — fill in a suitable feeling word. | I'm ______ to go to the coast! (a happy feeling) | I'm ______ because I lost my book. (a sad feeling) | My friend said she is excited. I said, “______!” (agree) | Part C — complete each sentence with the starter or pronoun in brackets. | ______ go to the museum this weekend! (Let's) | ______ need to help each other. (We) | ______ tired after running. (I feel) Answer key: Part A — 1) aren't you; 2) do they; 3) isn't she. Part B — 1) any happy feeling word works, for example excited or glad; 2) any sad feeling word works, for example sad or upset; 3) Me too! Part C — 1) Let's; 2) We; 3) I feel.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Invite a Friend
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Use would like to to invite someone. Get ready to say:
“Would you like to visit the museum with me?”
“Would you like to come to the event in my neighbourhood?”
“I would like to try the new restaurant. Would you like to come?”
Record yourself. Check: Did you say “would like to”? Did you sound polite and friendly?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play my friend while my adult helper listens, and tell me whether each invitation I make sounds polite and complete.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Tell Someone Your Plan
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Use going to to describe a plan for a trip. Say three sentences:
“On Saturday, I am going to ______.”
“We are going to arrive at the ______ at ______ o'clock.”
“After that, we are going to ______.”
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my three plan sentences and check that every one uses am, is or are before going to.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Where Am I?
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Play with your AI tutor or your family:
One person thinks of a place from the vocabulary list (station, mall, airport, museum …).
The other person asks yes/no questions: “Can you buy food there?” “Do trains stop there?”
Keep asking until you can say: “You are at the ______!” Then swap turns.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Think of one place from this unit and answer only yes or no while my adult helper keeps score of my guesses.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Vocabulary Expert Interview
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Choose six place words from this unit. Ask a clear question about each one, then answer six questions your partner asks you. Use complete sentences and say each word twice.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Interview me about customer, arrive, event, horizon, equator and rental, and mark any answer that is not a full sentence.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Explain and Respond
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Explain why Noah said the museum teaches more than the mall does. Give your reason with because, then answer two follow-up questions from your listener.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me two follow-up questions about the museum and the mall, and tell me if my reason after because really explains my opinion.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Three-Minute Unit Talk
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Plan and record a three-minute talk about a trip you would like to make. Open by naming your destination, give three connected ideas with details, and close by inviting your listener to come.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my three-minute talk with an adult nearby, then tell me which of my three ideas needed one more detail.

writing.title: Writing 1: A Tour Plan for Your Capital City
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Imagine you are showing a visitor around your capital city. Write a short paragraph (4–5 sentences) about the tour. Include at least three places, such as a museum, a restaurant, or the airport. Use going to and arrive.
Example opening: “First, we are going to visit the museum. We will arrive at ten o'clock …”
writing.modelText: A strong tour plan names three real places in a sensible order, gives a time for one of them, and uses going to at least twice.
writing.sentenceStarter: First, we are going to visit
writing.successCriteria: I named three places; I put them in order; I used going to twice; I used arrive with a time; I checked my capital letters and full stops
writing.support: List your three places first, then write one sentence for each before joining them.
writing.extension: Add a comparative adverb, such as we walk more slowly through the museum.

writing.title: Writing 2: An Invitation to an Event
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write an invitation to an event in your neighbourhood — maybe a harvest celebration, a market day, or a football match. Use would like to at least twice. Remember to say WHAT the event is, WHERE it is, and WHEN it is.
writing.modelText: A strong invitation opens warmly, states the what, where and when in separate sentences, and closes with a polite would like to question.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to invite you to
writing.successCriteria: I said what the event is; I said where it is; I said when it is; I used would like to twice; I stayed polite from start to finish
writing.support: Answer the three questions what, where and when on scrap paper before you write.
writing.extension: Add a question tag at the end, such as you will come, won't you?

writing.title: Writing 3: A Short Dialogue
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short dialogue (6–8 lines) between a customer and a worker at a bike rental shop. Use polite language and at least one imperative (an instruction).
writing.modelText: A strong dialogue gives each speaker a new line, uses speech marks correctly, and hides at least one imperative inside a helpful instruction.
writing.successCriteria: I started a new line for each speaker; I used speech marks; I used one imperative; I kept both speakers polite; I read my dialogue aloud
writing.support: Say the conversation out loud with a partner, then write down what you both said.
writing.extension: Add a price and a return time so the instruction becomes really useful.

writing.title: Writing 4: Compare Two Places
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a six-sentence paragraph comparing a museum and a mall. Begin with a topic sentence, then join your ideas with and, but and because.
writing.modelText: A strong comparison opens with a topic sentence, alternates between the two places, and finishes with the writer's own preference and reason.
writing.sentenceStarter: A museum and a mall are both busy, but
writing.successCriteria: I wrote a topic sentence; I gave three facts about each place; I used and, but and because; I ended with my own opinion; I checked my punctuation
writing.support: Draw two columns, fill each with three facts, then turn the rows into sentences.
writing.extension: Use a superlative adverb, such as the museum explains things most clearly.

writing.title: Writing 5: A Fact File About the Equator
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a heading and five accurate facts about living near the equator. Use the words nation, railroad and factories, then check your spelling and punctuation.
writing.modelText: A strong fact file uses a clear heading, numbers each fact, and keeps every sentence to one idea that a reader can check.
writing.successCriteria: I wrote a heading; I listed five facts; I used nation, railroad and factories; I kept each fact to one idea; I proofread my spelling
writing.support: Reread Living Near the Equator and underline five facts before you begin.
writing.extension: Add a sixth fact from your own reading and say where you found it.

writing.title: Writing 6: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Reread your tour plan. Rewrite three sentences with stronger adverbs, add two new details, and explain in one sentence which change helped the reader most.
writing.modelText: A strong reflection shows the old sentence beside the new one and names the exact improvement rather than saying it is better.
writing.successCriteria: I rewrote three sentences; I added two details; I chose stronger adverbs; I explained my best change; I copied my final version neatly
writing.support: Use a coloured pen so the new words stand out beside the old ones.
writing.extension: Ask a partner which change they noticed first, and record their answer.

activities.title: Activities 1: Match the Place to What You Do There
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Match each place (1–6) to the correct action (a–f).
1. airport
2. museum
3. restaurant
4. station
5. mall
6. office
a. eat a meal cooked for you
b. catch a train or a bus
c. work at a desk
d. see old things and learn about history
e. get on an aeroplane
f. shop in many stores under one roof

activities.title: Activities 2: Choose the Right Grammar
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write the correct choice for each sentence.
1. We are ______ (going to / would like) explore the capital tomorrow.
2. Would you ______ (like to / going to) visit the museum?
3. The train arrived ______ (fast / faster) than the bus.
4. You're coming to the event, ______ (aren't you / are you)?
5. ______ (Take / Taking) the elevator to the fifth floor.
activities.answerSummary: 1. going to 2. like to 3. faster 4. aren't you 5. Take.

activities.title: Activities 3: Fill in the Blanks (vocabulary)
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Complete each sentence with a word from the unit.
1. The main city of a country is its ______.
2. A person who buys something is a ______.
3. The line where the sky meets the sea is the ______.
4. A place where aeroplanes take off and land is an ______.
5. The area around your home is your ______.

activities.title: Activities 4: Sort the Places
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Sort sixteen unit words into three columns: places you travel to, places inside a town, and parts of a building. Write one sentence that explains the rule for each column.
activities.answerSummary: Travel: tourism, airport, station, railroad, capital, nation. Town: museum, mall, restaurant, office, factories, neighbourhood. Building: entrance, hallway, elevator, rental.

activities.title: Activities 5: Reading Evidence Hunt
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Find six details in this unit's texts that show how busy places work. Copy each detail and explain what it tells the reader about that place.
activities.answerSummary: Strong finds include the crowded streets caused by tourism, the glass elevator in the tall building, and the guide's remark about heat near the equator.

activities.title: Activities 6: Design a Direction Trail
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Design a short direction trail through a building using imperatives. Teach it to another learner and check that they reach the right room.
activities.answerSummary: A trail is complete when it names a starting point, uses at least three imperatives, and ends at one room the partner can find.

assignments.title: Places, People, and Plans learning portfolio
assignments.instructions: Submit Writing 1: A Tour Plan for Your Capital City together with a recording of Speaking 1: Invite a Friend. The tour plan must name three real places in order and use going to twice and arrive once with a time. The recording must contain two polite invitations that both use would like to. Marking: 16 marks for the writing against rub-writing-v1 and 16 marks for the recording against rub-speaking-v1. Award the top band only when the places follow a sensible route and the speaker stays polite from greeting to close; award the middle band when the language is accurate but the order of places is muddled.
assignments.sourceFile: Derived from unit writing and speaking tasks

quizzes.question: Which word means the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth?
quizzes.explanation: The horizon is where sea meets sky, a railroad is a track and an entrance is a doorway; only the equator circles the Earth.

quizzes.question: What does the word 'customer' mean?
quizzes.options: A person who buys something from a shop or business. | A machine that carries people up and down between floors. | The track that trains travel along. | The area around your home.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A person who buys something from a shop or business.
quizzes.explanation: A customer is a person, while the other three options describe a machine, a track and a place.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses 'would like to' correctly?
quizzes.options: I would like visit the museum. | I would like to visit the museum. | I would to like visit the museum. | I like would to visit the new museum.
quizzes.correctAnswer: I would like to visit the museum.
quizzes.explanation: The pattern is would like to plus the base verb, so to must sit directly before visit.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is a correct 'going to' plan?
quizzes.options: I going to play football. | I am going to play football. | I am go to play football tomorrow. | I going to playing football.
quizzes.correctAnswer: I am going to play football.
quizzes.explanation: A going to plan needs am, is or are before it, and the verb after to stays in its base form.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct adverb: The train arrived ______ than the bus.
quizzes.options: fastest | more fast | faster | most fast
quizzes.explanation: Fast is a short adverb, so it takes -er when two things are compared.

quizzes.question: Which tag completes the sentence? You're coming to the event, ______?
quizzes.options: are you | aren't you | do they | haven't you
quizzes.explanation: The sentence is positive and uses are, so the tag must be the negative aren't you.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'A Trip to the Capital': First, we went to the big _____ and waited for the train.
quizzes.explanation: The text says they went to the big station and waited for the train there.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'Living Near the Equator': Trains run on the _____, ships arrive at the coast, and factories make goods.
quizzes.explanation: Trains travel on a railroad; the other three options are places rather than tracks.

quizzes.question: Which line is a correct negative instruction for a busy building?
quizzes.options: Not run in the hallway. | You not run in the hallway. | Don't run in the hallway. | No running you in the long hallway.
quizzes.explanation: A negative imperative starts with don't and then the base verb, with no subject in front.

quizzes.question: In 'The Day We Got Lost in Mombasa', where did the children finally find their uncle?
quizzes.options: At the end of the hallway on the second floor | Beside the juice stand at the busy train station | Inside the museum beside the old maps and tools | On the fourth floor of the shopping mall
quizzes.correctAnswer: At the end of the hallway on the second floor
quizzes.explanation: The rental stand worker sent them up in the elevator, and the uncle stood at the end of the hallway.

liveSessions.title: Places, People, and Plans: Launch and the four word groups
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read the unit overview and tick the words you already know on the Word Wall.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min Word Wall warm-up; 10 min teacher models the four place groups; 15 min learners sort sixteen words into groups; 10 min partners describe a place without naming it; 5 min set the vocabulary target for the week
liveSessions.afterSession: Say five new place words aloud to an adult at home.

liveSessions.title: Places, People, and Plans: Reading the capital and the equator
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read A Trip to the Capital and Living Near the Equator once each.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min retrieval of place words; 10 min shared reading of the capital text; 15 min learners locate answers and underline evidence; 10 min paired comparison of the two texts; 5 min feedback on quoting evidence
liveSessions.afterSession: Answer comprehension questions 1 to 5 in full sentences.

liveSessions.title: Places, People, and Plans: Would like to and going to workshop
liveSessions.beforeSession: Complete Grammar 1 and Grammar 2 practice before the session.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min quick invitation round; 10 min teacher models would like to and going to side by side; 15 min guided correction of mixed sentences; 10 min partners plan a Saturday trip; 5 min feedback on the missing to
liveSessions.afterSession: Record three going to sentences about your own weekend.

liveSessions.title: Places, People, and Plans: Adverbs, imperatives and directions
liveSessions.beforeSession: Complete Grammar 3 and Grammar 5 practice before the session.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min adverb speed round; 10 min teacher models comparative adverbs in directions; 15 min learners build a direction trail through the school; 10 min partners follow each other's trails; 5 min feedback on precise adverbs
liveSessions.afterSession: Write your direction trail neatly for Activities 6.

liveSessions.title: Places, People, and Plans: Tour plan writing conference
liveSessions.beforeSession: Bring a first draft of the Writing 1 tour plan.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min share one strong opening; 10 min teacher models improving a weak plan; 15 min learners revise their own draft; 10 min partner check against the success criteria; 5 min set one revision target each
liveSessions.afterSession: Rewrite your tour plan with the change you agreed.

liveSessions.title: Places, People, and Plans: Story talk, question tags and Year 4 reflection
liveSessions.beforeSession: Reread The Day We Got Lost in Mombasa and note the moment you liked best.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min question tag greeting circle; 10 min discussion of why Amal stayed calm; 15 min group presentations about a place; 10 min unit quiz; 5 min Year 4 reflection and celebration
liveSessions.afterSession: Complete the unit quiz and the self-assessment.

teacherNotes.note: Model would like to and going to side by side before independent work, because learners mix the two when they mean a plan. An adult must be present whenever a learner uses the AI tutor, and no child should be left alone with the device during recording tasks. Offer the direction trail orally for learners who find writing tiring, and praise precise place words rather than long answers.

Reading and listening: ask the tutor to read the listening scripts aloud and then quiz the learner; ask it to play a directions game around the mall; ask it to explain any unfamiliar word in the reading texts.
Speaking: ask the tutor to practise polite invitations; ask it to play Where Am I? with hints; ask it to check the learner's going to sentences.
Writing: ask the tutor to check the tour plan; ask it to make the invitation sound more polite; ask it to act out the bike rental dialogue as the shop worker.
Vocabulary: ask the tutor to quiz the place words with a picture clue; ask it to say the capital city in a full sentence; ask it for two more sentences using tourism.
Grammar: ask the tutor to explain any wrong answer; ask it why aren't you follows You're coming; ask it for five more going to sentences.
All tutor work happens with an adult in the room.
